title: Bauhaus, speculative design, and the whole Earth
introduction: This week's session came in two halves that turned out to be about the same question. Ryan Bishop opened with the Bauhaus and its insistence that art, design, and technology are one practice, then arrived, through two contemporary works, at speculative design — design that raises questions instead of solving them. The guest, Bobby Pietrusko, spoke online from the University of Pennsylvania about four projects built around satellites and data, and how they shape the way we imagine 'the global'. Underneath both halves was a single question: what is design for, and whose picture of the world does it produce?
related_work:
Ryan told the Bauhaus as a story about refusing boundaries. Walter Gropius founded it in Weimar in 1919, it later moved to Dessau and then Berlin, and it was shut down in 1933 when the Nazis came to power. It was, from the start, an answer to the First World War: where Dada turned its back on the machine, the Bauhaus embraced industrial technology, and it held that there is no essential difference between art, design, architecture, and craft — a chair, a poster, and a painting were all one discipline. The ideal was equal admission for everyone, though reality fell short in a familiar way, and women were largely directed into weaving. The names that passed through it — Mies van der Rohe, Paul Klee, Kandinsky, Moholy-Nagy, Kepes, Josef and Anni Albers — mostly went into exile in America after the closure, and through them the Bauhaus fed into Harvard, MIT, and Black Mountain College.

From there Ryan moved to speculative design by way of two works. Extinction Gong, by Julian Oliver and collaborators, is a large gong wired to live data: each time a species is declared extinct, it is struck four times, and at the current rate of roughly twenty-seven thousand species a year that works out to about one every nineteen minutes. Rare Earthenware, by Liam Young and Unknown Fields, commissioned by the V&A, is three ceramic vases made from the toxic mud of a rare-earth tailings lake in Inner Mongolia, sized to match the waste produced in making a phone, a lightweight laptop, and an electric-car battery, with a companion film that runs the supply chain backwards to the mine. Both are speculative design, which took shape in the 1990s but has its roots in the systems theory and cybernetics of the 1930s. It is aimed at wicked problems, and it does not chase a final answer — it tries to raise a question, spark imagination, and set off collective action, through methods like scenario planning, narrative, and interdisciplinary collaboration, and examples that run from restoring wetlands in Britain to deep-sea mining. The line Ryan kept returning to was that design is meant to solve problems while art only presents them, and speculative design lives in the gap between the two.

The second half was Bobby Pietrusko on four projects that all circle satellites and the data they produce. In Plain Sight pairs the two most famous photographs of the Earth from space: the Blue Marble, which gave us the story of a fragile planet worth protecting, and the Black Marble, the night-time view, which tells the opposite story of globalisation and connected cities — and both come from the same satellite. Transactions began from the fact that the art world keeps no ready-made data, so his team hand-transcribed the biennale and auction catalogues from 1945 to 2010 into a database, and found a small number of curators touring a fixed roster of artists from show to show in order to push their prices up. Satellite Symphony draws on real-time data from more than two thousand ground stations and the satellites of many countries, which together recalculate the Earth's centre of mass every day — an offset of a few millimetres becomes tens or hundreds of metres once it reaches the surface. And the black-hole project went further still: synchronising radio telescopes across the planet and using the Earth's own rotation, so that the whole planet becomes a single telescope.

What stayed with me most was the way Pietrusko works. He does not reach for ready-made tools; each piece starts from a blank text file, and he writes his own software in C++ and OpenGL. He has also set students an exercise I found strange and then brilliant: think like a conspiracy theorist — that paranoid, everything-is-connected way of seeing — but point it at solving global problems instead of inventing them, his example being getting Coca-Cola to solve a drought. In the questions he was equally direct about the practical side: to begin programming, Python, Processing, or TouchDesigner with your own components are all fine; do not let an AI write your code, but throw your error messages at it and treat it like a tutor; and a rotating globe is just a sphere with a light source, a flat data map wrapped onto it as a texture, and a height map for the relief — the material editor in Blender can do it.
method: My method this week was to listen for the through-line rather than the facts. I treated the two speakers as one argument — Bauhaus to speculative design to satellites — and kept asking how each example answered the same question: what is design for, and who gets to decide what the world looks like. Then I tested it against my own project.
results_discussion:
The idea I keep turning over is that speculative design does not try to answer a problem but to raise a question and set people moving. That is hard for me, because my instinct is always to build toward a finished thing. But it reframes my own project: instead of asking what the piece should be, I can ask what question it should make people sit with, and let the answer stay open. The window theme my partner and I settled on now feels like a question rather than a product, which is more honest about what the work actually is.

Pietrusko unsettled me in a different way. He starts each piece from a blank text file and writes his own software, which is the exact opposite of how I work — I reach for a tool that already does most of it. I am not ready to give up ready-made tools, but the point is not the language; it is that he refuses to let the tool decide what the work can be. The two Earth photographs made the same argument: the Blue Marble and the Black Marble come from the same satellite, yet one tells a story of a fragile planet and the other of a connected one. The image is not neutral, and neither is the tool. That sits close to my new project idea about people and nature, which is itself a story about how we picture the natural world and where we place ourselves inside the picture.
conclusion_future_work: My takeaways are to carry speculative design's discipline of asking-before-solving into my own project, and to keep questioning what my tools and images are silently deciding for me. The practical notes help too: Python, Processing, or TouchDesigner as a starting point, an AI used as a tutor for error messages rather than a ghostwriter, and the Blender recipe for a rotating globe. Next I want to sketch the people-and-nature idea as a question rather than a solution, and see what the projection work looks like once it is trying to ask something.
